name: Clip-on sunglass lenses

lead:
Clip-on sunglass lenses are tinted lens covers that fasten onto the front of regular eyeglasses, usually by a clip or by magnets. They turn prescription frames into sunglasses in a few seconds and come off again indoors.
For appearance, they let glasses wearers adopt the sunglasses look and its face-framing effect, and they cover the eyes against glare. Wikipedia lists clip-ons and flip-up designs as the two ways of adding sunglasses to corrective eyewear.

paras: The wearer attaches the clip-on over the existing frame when outside and removes it indoors. Some designs use a hinge so the tint flips up; others use magnets or a spring clip. They are chosen to match the frame's size and shape.

Risks are practical: a poor fit can scratch lenses or slip, and tint and UV protection vary by product. Standards such as ISO 12312 govern sunglass performance generally, so labels are the guide to UV blocking.

Wearer gets the sunglasses look without a second pair
angle.text: They give glasses wearers a quick way to wear shades over their prescription frames, which changes how the face is framed. The lenses come off again indoors.

lead: Clip-on sunglass lenses are tinted lenses that attach to the front of prescription eyeglasses, turning them into sunglasses without a second prescription pair. Wikipedia describes clip-ons and flip-up lenses as the two designs for adding sun protection to corrective glasses.[1]

In looksmaxxing and style discussion, they matter because sunglasses are both protective eyewear and a fashion accessory,[1] and clip-ons let glasses wearers take part in that look. The covered eyes, the frame line and the lens shape all change how the upper face reads.

Sunglasses themselves have a long history: smoky quartz lenses in China by the 12th century, tinted spectacles in Venice, UV-shielding glass around 1899, mass-produced celluloid pairs from 1929 and polarised lenses in 1936.[1] No published clinical studies of clip-on lenses were found.

paras: Clip-ons are separate tinted lenses that clip onto ordinary frames, and flip-ups are tinted lenses hinged to the glasses so they can be raised indoors.[1] Magnetic versions, sold by many eyewear makers, are a variant of the same idea.

Tinted lenses appeared in Venice in the 18th century, and by the 1750s were being tested for vision correction.[1] Interest in UV blocking grew from the late 1800s, Sam Foster began mass-producing celluloid sunglasses in 1929, and by 1938 Life magazine described sunglasses as a fashion fad.[1]

timeline.event: Rodenstock may have made the first UV-shielding sunglasses.[1]
Sam Foster begins mass-producing celluloid sunglasses.[1]
